paras: Wilson Prado started as a lawyer thirty-one years ago, and in the first eighteen of those years he never opened a document in English. His firm used to be three rooms above a bakery in Ribeirao Preto. The work was domestic: land, family companies, the occasional dispute between two neighbors who knew each other from school. He used to know every judge in the district by name, and he says that used to be the whole job.

The turning point was not a decision. It was a client. In 2011 a sugar mill that his firm advised for ten years signed its first export contract, and the buyer was Swiss. Wilson did not use to read contracts in English, and he did not use to work with anybody outside the state. Within two years half of his caseload had a foreign party on the other side, and the three rooms above the bakery were now an office with eleven people in it.

He is honest about the cost. He used to leave at six and have dinner with his children. Now the calls from Europe start before eight in the morning and the ones from Asia end after ten at night, and that lifestyle is not something anybody chooses on purpose. He also used to be the person in the room who knew the most, and for about three years he was not. He says that was harder than the hours.

Younger lawyers ask him whether it was worth it, and his answer is always the same two sentences. The work is more interesting than it used to be, and he is more tired than he used to be. Then he adds the part they do not expect: he started at forty-four, and the language was never the real obstacle. The real obstacle was admitting, in front of people twenty years younger, that he did not understand something.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a Brazilian practice that went international, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how to open a law firm in a small city.
To show how one practice changed shape, what it cost, and what the real obstacle turned out to be.
To argue that lawyers should learn English before they are forty.

items.situation: Say two things about his practice that were true before 2011 and are not true now.
tips: He used to know every judge by name, and the firm used to be three rooms above a bakery.
Both are states that ended. That is exactly what used to is for.

items.situation: Now the same in the negative. Two things he did not do before.
tips: He did not use to read contracts in English, and he did not use to work outside the state.
Careful: after did, it is use to, without the D.

items.situation: Ask me two questions about how my work used to be.
tips: Did you use to travel a lot? Did you use to work on weekends?
Not: did you used to. The did already carries the past.

items.situation: Correct me. I say: 'I use to work only with domestic clients.'
tips: I used to work only with domestic clients.
Without the D it is a present tense, and that is not what you mean.

items.situation: Your own practice. Two things that used to be true and are not any more.
tips: I used to handle only Brazilian contracts. My firm used to have one office.
This is the sentence an admission interview asks for, in other words.

items.situation: One habit you did NOT use to have, and now you do.
tips: I did not use to read the news in English in the morning, and now I do it every day.

listenings.text: People ask me what changed, and I always start with the calendar, because that is where you see it first. I used to have one diary and it fitted in my pocket. Meetings were in the morning, court was in the afternoon, and nothing ever happened on a Sunday. I did not use to think about time zones at all. Today my first message arrives at seven, from somebody in Rotterdam who has already had lunch, and my last one arrives after ten, from Singapore. The work itself is not more difficult than it used to be. The difficult part is that it never stops arriving. And here is the thing nobody warns you about: I do not miss the old caseload, and I do miss the old calendar. Those are two different feelings, and you are allowed to have both.

Thirty years ago a commodity lawyer in this country used to be a specialist in Brazilian law who occasionally saw a document from abroad. That job does not really exist any more. The contracts moved, the arbitration moved, and the language of both of them moved with them. So today the same lawyer has to keep up with three legal systems instead of one. I am not going to tell you that this is better or worse. I will tell you the part that matters for anybody thinking about starting late. The people who made that change well were almost never the youngest. They were the ones who already knew the business by heart and only had to learn the words. Learning the words is slow, but it is finite. Learning the business takes twenty years.
